claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been produced in a hierarchical heterostructured state featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A hybrid machine-learning framework can integrate multiscale structural descriptors with reduced-order thermophysical parameters.

The proposed framework can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately and cheaply than first-principles, CALPHAD, or full-scale MD methods.
Interface density, chemical-fluctuation amplitude, sub-domain size, and related features can be quantified through image analysis or low-cost simulations.
A modest set of high-accuracy experimental and simulation data is sufficient to train the proposed regression model.
The model is intended to apply at room temperature and conventional strain rates to samples retaining the validated hierarchical state.
The model's domain is restricted to alloys having phase distributions and chemical-fluctuation scales similar to those represented in its training data.
Interface density, sub-domain size, and chemical fluctuations mediate dislocation motion.
The same microstructural markers mediate crack deflection.
Changes in dislocation motion and crack deflection govern the alloy's macroscopic elastic, yield, and fracture behavior.
Physics-informed descriptors can map the hierarchical microstructure into a low-dimensional representation correlated with the three target mechanical properties.
This low-dimensional representation reduces reliance on computationally expensive full-scale simulations while maintaining physical fidelity.
Prediction errors for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness will be approximately 10-15% relative to experiments.
The framework will be at least ten times more computationally efficient than full first-principles or CALPHAD approaches.
Ab initio and MD calculations are time-consuming, and CALPHAD may require significant computational resources.
Traditional first-principles, CALPHAD, and high-fidelity MD methods typically have prediction errors of at least 20% for the three target properties.
Model reliability will degrade for out-of-distribution hierarchical descriptors or microstructures.
Extreme processing, microstructural evolution, unexpected phases, or a change in the dominant deformation mechanism can invalidate the model.
Directly mapping hierarchical microstructure to toughness is especially difficult.
The proposed benchmark falsifies the hypothesis if any target-property error exceeds 15% or if computational speedup is less than tenfold.
